content: In Nepal, cigarette packs that do not comply with the 90% pictorial health warning (PHW) requirement are still being sold. However, no punitive measures have been taken against the manufacturers, as the law does not impose penalties on wholesalers and retailers for violations. This delay in enforcement benefits the tobacco industry. For instance, in the Maldives, although the Attorney General approved PHW legislation requiring 75% warnings in September 2017, the law was only endorsed and gazetted in January 2019, after more than a year of delay influenced by the tobacco industry. Governments also provide financial benefits to the tobacco industry, such as tax exemptions and subsidies. In the 2017-2018 fiscal year, the Nepalese government retained value-added tax (VAT) exemptions for unprocessed tobacco. In India, under the Goods and Services Tax (GST) regime, tax exemptions for bidi manufacturers were expanded from units producing less than two million sticks to those with an annual turnover of less than INR 2 million. Indonesia, which is not a party to the Framework Convention on Tobacco Control (FCTC), continues to make decisions favoring the tobacco industry, such as allowing tobacco advertisements on television. A 2017 draft bill in Indonesia’s Parliament included a clause to ban tobacco advertisements in broadcast media, but this clause was removed during the legislative process, allowing cigarette advertising to continue. Efforts to simplify complex taxation systems have also been blocked by the tobacco industry. For example, in some countries, recommendations to streamline a 12-tiered taxation system were rejected after the tobacco industry argued that it would increase smuggling, harm small-scale producers, and reduce government revenue. As a result, tobacco companies continue to thrive and increase their profits. In Timor-Leste, Nepal, and Thailand, governments do not engage in partnerships with the tobacco industry or accept assistance from it for tobacco control activities. However, unnecessary interactions with the tobacco industry still occur in some countries. For example, in Bangladesh, British American Tobacco (BAT) received a corporate governance award from the Institute of Chartered Secretaries of Bangladesh. Transparency remains a significant issue, as many countries lack procedures for disclosing meetings with the tobacco industry, and records of such interactions are not made public. Additionally, there are no rules requiring the registration or disclosure of tobacco industry entities, affiliated organizations, or lobbyists. In Indonesia, interactions with the tobacco industry are more overt. Several ministers and senior government officials have attended events organized by the tobacco industry. The Directorate General of Customs and Excise supported an education program on preventing illegal cigarette trading, which was part of a campaign launched by tobacco industry associations. In Nepal, no senior government officials currently serve on the boards of tobacco companies, nor have retired officials joined the industry. However, in other countries, there are instances where senior officials have joined the tobacco industry while still in office or after retirement. In Thailand, retired senior government officials are regularly appointed as members of the monopoly board of the Tobacco Authority of Thailand (TAOT). Current government officials, such as those from the Excise Department and Ministry of Finance, also serve on the TAOT board. In India, the board of directors of the India Tobacco Company (ITC) includes individuals linked to various government departments and ministries. In Bangladesh, high-level government officials hold positions in BAT Bangladesh, creating conflicts of interest as they promote the tobacco business while advancing tobacco control agendas. Most countries in the region do not have policies prohibiting contributions from the tobacco industry to political parties, candidates, or campaigns. Myanmar is an exception, as it has implemented such a policy. Some progress has been made in implementing preventive measures. For example, Thailand’s Ministry of Public Health has developed guidelines for interacting with the tobacco industry, which will be extended to the entire government. However, many countries still lack systems to monitor the tobacco industry’s dealings with the government or procedures for disclosing records of such interactions. While some governments have formulated policies to reduce interactions, codes of conduct have not yet been developed. In Indonesia, the Ministry of Health has issued guidelines on interactions with the tobacco industry, but these need to be extended to other departments to advance tobacco control. The Maldives’ Tobacco Control Law includes a procedure for disclosing interactions with the tobacco industry, and a code of conduct for government institutions is being drafted. However, implementing regulations are not yet in place. Timor-Leste, like the Maldives, lacks procedures or guidelines for meetings between government officials and representatives of foreign tobacco companies. Bangladesh and Sri Lanka have not established procedures for disclosing records of interactions with the tobacco industry or adopted codes of conduct for public officials. To protect tobacco control policies, governments should take immediate steps, including banning tobacco-related corporate social responsibility (CSR) activities and other contributions from the tobacco industry. Partial restrictions, such as prohibiting publicity of these activities, have proven ineffective. Retired senior government officials should not be immediately appointed to the tobacco industry, and former tobacco industry executives should not be appointed to government positions. Transparency in interactions with the tobacco industry must be improved, with clear procedures and public disclosure of all records. Governments should adopt codes of conduct to guide officials in dealing with the tobacco industry and require tobacco companies to periodically submit information on production, marketing expenditures, revenues, lobbying, philanthropy, and political contributions.
